claim: Define your specialism by the class of problem you solve (huge product catalogues, tangled navigation, poor conversion) rather than by industry vertical, so the same expertise transfers across every client type.
why: A problem-based specialism compounds: each project deepens the same skill, and it stays relevant no matter what sector the next client sells in, whereas a niche-based specialism resets when the niche dries up.
when: Positioning a design practice, writing a portfolio or service page, or deciding which projects to take on.
fails: The problem class is so narrow or rare that too few clients have it, or when a vertical genuinely carries hard-won domain knowledge (regulated industries, complex compliance) that outweighs the transferable-skill benefit.

claim: Before proposing an add-on service, locate the actual bottleneck in the client's funnel — traffic in, or conversion of that traffic — and propose the service that fixes the constrained stage.
why: Improving an already-abundant input yields almost nothing; the return sits entirely at whichever stage is limiting outcomes.
when: Scoping a redesign for a business with measurable commercial outcomes, where you can see or ask for traffic and conversion numbers.
fails: You have no visibility into the client's metrics, or the site is new with both weak traffic and weak conversion — then acquisition usually has to come first because there is nothing to optimise against.

claim: For a site already receiving high traffic volume, choose conversion rate optimisation over SEO as the paid add-on.
why: The site has already solved acquisition; the unexploited gain is in the percentage of existing visitors who buy.
when: Established e-commerce, creator merch stores, or any site with a large existing audience and a transactional goal.
fails: Traffic is low, seasonal, or the wrong audience entirely — in that case more or better-qualified visitors is the higher-leverage fix.

claim: Justify your fee by translating the proposed improvement into the client's own revenue arithmetic — percentage lift multiplied by their current volume — instead of pricing by hours or deliverables.
why: At scale, a marginal percentage improvement produces an absolute revenue figure that dwarfs your fee, which makes the price obviously worth paying rather than something to negotiate down.
when: Pitching optimisation or redesign work to a client with existing volume and a measurable transaction value.
fails: The client has no baseline numbers to multiply against, or the outcome is not directly monetisable (brand sites, portfolios, internal tools), where value has to be argued another way.

claim: Bundle one or two adjacent, semi-related services with the core design work — but only ones that attack the same underlying problem the design is meant to solve.
why: Related services are what differentiate you from designers offering identical visual deliverables, and they let you own the client's outcome rather than just their layout; unrelated add-ons read as upselling.
when: Building a service menu or writing a proposal where you need to justify a higher price than competing designers.
fails: The add-on is outside your competence or unconnected to the client's stated goal, which dilutes your positioning and creates delivery risk.

claim: When two plausible services could both be offered, ask which one the client would pay extra for, and lead the proposal with that one.
why: Willingness to pay is a proxy for perceived leverage; leading with the high-leverage service anchors the engagement around outcomes rather than around aesthetics.
when: Structuring a proposal with multiple possible scopes.

claim: When a product pairs a user with a stranger, rate the interaction style itself (talkativeness, formality, pace) as a first-class attribute, not just competence or outcome quality.
why: The anxiety in these transactions is usually social, not functional; users already form a private guess about how the interaction will go, so a shown score removes guesswork the interface was silently leaving to them.
when: Marketplace, gig, or service products where a matched human shares time or space with the user — rides, home services, tutoring, care, sales calls.
fails: The trait is genuinely personal rather than service-relevant, or the score becomes a de facto performance metric that penalises the rated worker; also fails when the user has no way to act on the information.

claim: Always print the sample size next to a rating (e.g. '3.0 from 134 reviews') rather than the score alone.
why: A number without a denominator is unfalsifiable; the count is what lets a user decide whether to trust the score or ignore it.
when: Any aggregate score shown to users — ratings, match percentages, confidence scores.
fails: Counts are so low they undermine the feature's credibility — below a threshold, suppress the score instead of showing a noisy one.

claim: Reuse the scale and visual form of the rating the product already has when introducing a second rated dimension.
why: A '3 out of 5' reads instantly because the user has already been trained on the star rating in the same card; a novel scale would need explaining and would compete with the existing one.
when: Adding a secondary metric to a surface that already displays a primary rating.
fails: The new dimension is not actually ordinal — a preference like 'prefers quiet / happy to chat' is a category, and forcing it onto a 1-5 axis implies more chat is better.

claim: Attach new decision-support information to the exact screen state where the user can still act on it — here, the driver-matched card during the wait, not a settings page or post-trip summary.
why: The wait between match and pickup is dead time the user is already staring at, and it is the last moment they can mentally prepare or cancel; information delivered earlier has no subject and later has no use.
when: Inserting contextual detail into an existing flow with a defined waiting or confirmation state.
fails: The added row pushes the primary action (cancel, contact, track) below the fold or competes with safety-critical details like plate number.

claim: Design for the awkwardness in a flow, not only the task — name the emotional failure state ('the silent moments') and ship the smallest UI element that defuses it.
why: Flows are usually optimised until the task completes reliably, leaving the social discomfort around the task untouched even though it is what users actually remember.
when: Mature flows where the functional problem is solved and the remaining friction is emotional or interpersonal.
fails: The discomfort is better solved by a direct control (a 'quiet ride' toggle) than by more information for the user to interpret.

claim: If you ship a randomize/surprise-me action, seed it from the user's own history rather than from the full catalogue, so every result is plausible enough to accept.
why: Randomness over an unfiltered catalogue produces results the user must undo, which costs more effort than the manual path it was meant to replace; constraining the random draw to known preferences makes most outcomes acceptable as-is.
when: Any generate/shuffle/surprise-me control in a product where the user already has behavioural history and the output requires their approval.
fails: Cold-start users with no history, or contexts where discovery of the genuinely unfamiliar is the point (music, recipes, style inspiration) and personalised randomness would just echo what the user already knows.

claim: Any action that assembles a multi-item order on the user's behalf must display the running monetary total at the moment of assembly, not only at checkout.
why: When the system chooses the items, the user has no mental model of the cost, so cost becomes invisible until a screen where reversing it is expensive; showing the total inline keeps the consequence attached to the action.
when: Bulk-add, auto-fill, reorder, or bundle actions in commerce and any flow where a single tap commits real money.

claim: Before adding a one-tap shortcut, check that its failure mode is cheaper than the manual work it removes; if undoing the shortcut costs more than doing the task by hand, cut the feature.
why: A shortcut's value is the time saved minus the time spent correcting bad outputs; a one-click action that produces mostly-wrong results inverts that arithmetic and makes the product slower to use.
when: Evaluating automation, quick actions, or AI-generated defaults during feature triage.
fails: Low-stakes, easily dismissed suggestions where a wrong result costs a glance, so a low hit rate is still net positive.

claim: When porting an interaction from another context, re-evaluate it at your product's actual transaction size; a gesture that works at coffee-money scale does not survive being scaled to a hundred-dollar basket.
why: The social and financial stakes of an interaction scale with the value it moves, so the same mechanic that reads as a small kindness at one price point reads as a serious, irreversible commitment at another.
when: Borrowing a proven pattern from a different industry, price tier, or transaction volume.

claim: Do not design features whose cost lands on a third party — the fulfilment worker, the recipient, the moderator — who never opted into the interaction and cannot decline it.
why: The interaction is only pleasant for the initiator; everyone downstream absorbs the ambiguity and extra handling, which turns a novelty feature into recurring operational friction.
when: Any gift, share, transfer, or on-behalf-of flow that pulls a person outside the initiating user into the transaction.
fails: Flows with explicit recipient consent and a clear decline path, where the third party has agreed to participate before anything is committed.

claim: Place high-consequence or novelty actions away from the checkout path; the step immediately before payment should only contain controls that confirm or correct the existing order.
why: Users move through checkout in a low-attention confirmation mode, so an unrelated action inserted there is likely to be triggered without deliberation on a screen where mistakes are costly.
when: Laying out cart, checkout, and payment-confirmation screens.
fails: Genuinely order-relevant upsells such as delivery-speed upgrades or tips, which belong in checkout because they modify the transaction in front of the user.

claim: When a streak or progress counter is visible on a screen users open despite having lapsed, treat the broken state as a first-class design case — show the lapse without shaming, and give a one-tap path back into the activity rather than a reset-to-zero dead end.
why: A counter is only motivating while it is intact; once broken it becomes a permanent reminder of failure on every visit, which pushes users away from the very behaviour it was meant to encourage.
when: Habit, streak, or daily-goal features in content apps where lapses are the common case, not the exception.
fails: Products where the streak is the core game loop and losing it is the intended stake (competitive fitness, language drills with committed users) — softening the break removes the tension the product runs on.

claim: Do not gate access to a user's own content behind a task they must complete first; if you add a friction step, make skipping it a visible control on the same screen, not a hidden setting.
why: Content the user already owns and was in the middle of is not a reward to be earned; any interstitial between them and it is a tax, so the exit must be as reachable as the task itself.
when: Any interstitial, quiz, upsell, or engagement mechanic inserted between opening an app and resuming the primary activity.
fails: Genuine security or safety gates (auth, age checks, destructive-action confirmations), where an easy skip defeats the purpose.

claim: Ship any novel or opinionated engagement mechanic with an in-context off switch placed directly on the screen where the mechanic appears, sized and positioned so a first-time user can find it without opening settings.
why: Designers cannot predict which users will find a mechanic charming versus punishing; a local kill switch converts a potentially rage-inducing feature into an opt-out, preserving trust from the users it doesn't land with.
when: Introducing gamification, nudges, mini-games, or personality-driven interruptions into an established utility app.
fails: Core flows where opting out would leave the product incoherent — there, the answer is to not ship the mechanic rather than to bury an off switch.

claim: For imprecise recall tasks, use a continuous drag control (slider) that accepts unlimited attempts and reveals feedback per attempt, rather than a discrete input that can be scored wrong.
why: Users have a fuzzy sense of position, not an exact value; a draggable range plus retries turns a fail-state quiz into a narrowing search, so the interaction reads as playful rather than punitive.
when: Asking users to estimate a position, quantity, or point in a continuous range from memory.
fails: When the answer must be exact or a single attempt carries consequence — unlimited retries make the task meaningless and users will brute-force it.

claim: When stacking multiple escape routes on one screen, order them by increasing finality — the low-commitment out (finish this instance) above the permanent one (never show this again) — and let the more drastic option sit below where it reads as the stronger statement.
why: Users reach for the mildest resolution first; presenting escalation in order lets them resolve at the lowest level of commitment they actually need, and reserves the permanent choice for genuine rejection.
when: Dismissal patterns for recurring prompts, nudges, or interstitials with more than one exit.
fails: Single-exit dialogs, or cases where offering a permanent opt-out this early trains users to disable features they'd otherwise grow to like.

claim: Design engagement mechanics around what the lapsed user needs (re-entry, orientation, a reason to come back) instead of around punishing the behaviour you want to discourage.
why: Punishment mechanics assume the user's absence was a choice they can be corrected out of; in practice absence is usually circumstance, so the punishment lands on someone already inclined to leave and accelerates churn.
when: Retention and re-engagement design for consumer apps with self-directed, low-obligation activities like reading.
fails: Contexts with real external stakes where a consequence is the point (accountability apps, commitments the user explicitly bought into).

claim: Before designing any screen, write down the one action or outcome the user came for, and treat that statement as the acceptance test for every subsequent decision.
why: A design brief anchored in visual taste has no falsifiable success condition; one anchored in intent gives every element a pass/fail criterion.
when: Starting any interface whose purpose is to move a person toward a decision, task, or conversion.
fails: Exploratory or open-ended surfaces (browsing, feeds, brand experiences) where there is no single intent to name and forcing one flattens the design.

claim: Justify each decorative effect — 3D scenes, scroll-driven animation, elaborate transitions — by naming how it helps the user reach their goal; remove it if the only answer is that it looks impressive.
why: Ornament competes for the same attention the primary action needs, so unbudgeted flair is a net cost to task completion.
when: Any conversion-oriented or task-oriented page where a specific next step exists.
fails: The audience is a peer or industry one — portfolios, awards submissions, studio sites — where craft display is itself the goal.

claim: Identify who the real audience is (end users versus other designers) before setting the visual ambition level, and let that answer set the flair budget.
why: The two audiences reward opposite things — users reward clarity and speed, peers reward technical difficulty — so a single default standard will underserve one of them.
when: Setting direction at the start of a project, or defending a stylistic choice in critique.
fails: Projects that genuinely serve both audiences at once, such as a product marketing site for a design tool, where the tension has to be balanced rather than resolved.

claim: Sequence a page as an ordered narrative — a setup, a progression, and a resolution that is the call to action — rather than as a grid of independently attractive sections.
why: Framing layout as story forces each section to earn its position by advancing the reader toward the action, instead of standing alone as decoration.
when: Landing pages, onboarding flows, and any multi-section scroll experience.
fails: Reference-style surfaces such as dashboards, documentation, or settings, where users enter at arbitrary points and linear sequence is irrelevant.

claim: Reduce the primary content-consumption flow to one obvious action when the system can reliably choose the next item.
why: Removing competing controls lowers decision effort and cognitive load, making continuous use feel seamless.
when: A feed or sequence can be personalized well enough that users do not need to manually select every next item.
fails: When users need deliberate control, comparison, or access to diverse choices; a single-path flow can become opaque or restrictive.

claim: Use a short onboarding preference prompt as an initial signal, then quickly prioritize observed behavior and content-level signals to refine recommendations.
why: Stated preferences are useful but incomplete; interaction data and understanding the content itself can reveal interests users did not articulate.
when: Designing personalized recommendations with enough early interactions and content metadata to learn from.
fails: When behavioral data is sparse, consent is absent, or the inferred signals are unreliable or privacy-inappropriate.

claim: Design recommendation systems to discover likely future interests instead of treating initial preference selections as fixed instructions.
why: The chapter argues that a system can sometimes surface content a person engages with more than content they explicitly requested.
when: The product can test and evaluate recommendations while preserving an easy way to redirect or correct them.
fails: When the cost of an incorrect recommendation is high or users expect strict, explicit control over what is shown.

claim: When the core value is discovery across many interests, design content units for very fast consumption and immediate switching to a different topic.
why: Short units let people sample many unrelated subjects in one session, making breadth rather than depth the product’s differentiator.
when: Building a feed or discovery product intended for frequent, high-volume browsing.
fails: Users need sustained explanation, complex task completion, or deep learning from each item.

claim: Align the content format with the consumption cadence the interface encourages: a rapid feed needs a plentiful supply of concise, self-contained items.
why: A high daily consumption rate depends on enough distinct content to keep successive items varied and available.
when: Designing algorithmically ordered entertainment or discovery feeds with continuous sessions.
fails: The product has a limited catalogue or gains value from revisiting long, connected content.

claim: Pair a content platform with a free, purpose-built creation tool that lets non-experts produce publishable work quickly.
why: Reducing equipment, software-cost, and editing-skill barriers increases the number of people able to contribute quality content.
when: A product’s value depends on a steady supply of user-generated content.
fails: The platform cannot meaningfully distribute, reward, or help creators reach an audience after they create.

claim: Design creator tools to feel polished and simple enough that using them is itself an attraction to the ecosystem.
why: A sleek, accessible tool makes creation feel attainable rather than like professional production work.
when: You want consumers who normally only browse to try creating.

claim: Create an ecosystem loop in which consumption exposes users to creation tools, and creation generates more content for consumption.
why: Each new creator adds content that attracts and retains viewers, some of whom can become creators in turn.
when: Adjacent products can share a user base and naturally feed one another.
fails: The handoff between consuming and creating is hidden, cumbersome, or offers no compelling benefit.

claim: After a creator publishes, surface clear engagement and distribution signals quickly so they can tell that the platform has received and acted on their work.
why: Prompt visible response reduces uncertainty and gives users evidence that their action produced an outcome.
when: Designing publishing, submission, upload, or creator workflows where users wait to see whether their work reaches others.
fails: Do not fabricate or overstate engagement merely to create reassurance; the signals must reflect real activity or accurately communicate processing status.

claim: Make lightweight content easy to consume when the product depends on fast feedback between audiences and creators.
why: When each item demands little viewer commitment, more people can sample it, creating more opportunities for engagement and discovery.
when: Building feed-based media experiences where rapid viewing and creator feedback are central to the product loop.
fails: This is less suitable for content that needs depth, careful evaluation, or sustained attention before a meaningful response is possible.

claim: Treat credible opportunities for new creators to reach large audiences as a core creator-experience feature, not only as an algorithmic outcome.
why: The prospect of meaningful reach makes contributing feel worthwhile, especially for inexperienced users.
when: Designing creator platforms that need to attract and retain contributors with little existing audience.
fails: It breaks down if exposure is too unpredictable or opaque for creators to understand how participation can lead to results.

claim: Turn multi-step tasks into clearly completable milestones so users can see and pursue unfinished work.
why: Visible incompleteness can motivate people to finish a task.
when: An app has optional setup, onboarding, learning paths, or other multi-step user work.
fails: The milestone is manipulative, irrelevant, or asks for unnecessary user effort.

claim: Use one consistent in-app currency to record effort and make accumulated progress feel tangible.
why: A shared currency gives repeated actions a recognizable sense of advancement and can support unlocks.
when: Users perform recurring actions over time, such as lessons, tasks, or contributions.
fails: Points have no understandable purpose, feedback, or value to the user.

claim: Expose both completed progress and remaining work with clear progress indicators.
why: Knowing where users are and how far they have left to go makes accomplishments and next actions visible.
when: A goal can be divided into units, stages, or a measurable path.
fails: Progress is misleading, overly granular, or not meaningfully connected to completion.

claim: Add social mechanics such as leaderboards or public badges only when comparison reinforces the desired behavior.
why: Seeing relative standing and receiving recognition can encourage continued participation.
when: The activity has an appropriate peer group and social comparison is motivating rather than harmful.
fails: Competition discourages beginners, creates unhealthy pressure, or exposes users who expect privacy.

claim: Make rewards advance a real user goal rather than offering arbitrary collectibles.
why: Rewards motivate only when users see them as useful or meaningful.
when: Designing points, badges, unlocks, redemption systems, or completion incentives.
fails: The reward is disconnected from the task or has no perceived value.

claim: Anchor the system on a small set of repeatable core actions, and award a visible progress currency whenever users complete them.
why: A direct action-to-XP link makes ordinary participation feel like measurable advancement.
when: Designing a product with a recurring primary task, such as learning, fitness, productivity, or practice.
fails: When the rewarded action does not represent meaningful user value; users may optimize the metric instead of the intended outcome.

claim: Give earned progress currency a clear purpose, such as rank progression or eligibility for rewards, even if it is not directly spendable.
why: XP can motivate through status and unlocks rather than functioning as a purchase currency.
when: You want frequent feedback and long-term progression without attaching every reward to a store.
fails: When rank or unlocks are too remote, unclear, or unimportant to the user.

claim: Use separate currencies for distinct motivational roles: one for progress and one for spending on optional advantages or recovery tools.
why: Separating status progression from utility spending creates multiple connected reward loops.
when: A product has both ongoing progress tracking and optional consumables, boosts, or second-chance mechanics.
fails: When multiple currencies make the system difficult to understand or feel manipulative.

claim: Pair errors with an immediate, bounded penalty that creates stakes while allowing users to continue.
why: Losing a heart makes incorrect answers consequential without ending the broader progression loop.
when: Tasks have clear success or failure feedback and light friction can encourage attention or persistence.
fails: When mistakes are common because of ambiguity, accessibility needs, or an early learning curve.

claim: Make a daily streak easy to preserve through one meaningful recurring action, then reinforce its visibility with reminders.
why: A simple daily threshold turns return behavior into a continuity goal.
when: Daily use is genuinely beneficial and the product can provide value in short sessions.
fails: When daily cadence is unnecessary or reminders create guilt, fatigue, or unhealthy engagement pressure.

claim: Reward milestones with both recognition and a useful benefit.
why: Achievements acknowledge exceptional effort while gem rewards feed back into the utility economy.
when: You want to reinforce notable progress beyond the standard completion loop.
fails: When milestones are arbitrary, too frequent, or rewards dilute the value of normal progress.

claim: Choose a gamification concept where the core user behavior is measurable and can be rewarded repeatedly, rather than copying a well-established gamified category.
why: A differentiated domain gives the product more room to establish a distinct value proposition while reliable behavior data enables a meaningful reward loop.
when: Selecting a product area for a new gamified app or feature.
fails: The chosen domain cannot provide trustworthy behavior signals or the rewards would encourage harmful behavior.

claim: Anchor a financial-product game loop to real progress: let users set concrete goals, reward verified contributions, preserve streaks for repeated action, and award larger completion rewards for larger goals.
why: The loop connects recurring saving behavior to immediate feedback and a longer-term milestone, making progress feel visible and motivating.
when: Designing engagement mechanics for savings or other goal-based financial behavior.
fails: Reward levels are not calibrated to goal difficulty or users can game contributions without making meaningful progress.

claim: Model multiple goal allocations as virtual accounts when users typically have a single underlying savings account.
why: Separating one balance into labelled goal buckets lets people understand progress toward several intentions without requiring separate real-world bank accounts.
when: A financial interface needs to support concurrent savings goals over one connected account balance.
fails: The interface implies that virtual allocations are separate protected bank balances when they are only planning categories.

claim: Use a normalized competitive measure for social ranking when users have unequal financial circumstances.
why: Raw savings totals would favor people with higher incomes or stronger currencies, undermining the perceived fairness of a leaderboard.
when: Adding leaderboards or comparative rewards to financial products with varied user incomes, locations, or currencies.
fails: The normalization formula is opaque, inaccurate, or exposes sensitive financial information.

claim: Pair behavioral rewards with practical feedback and education, including spending and savings analytics, visual challenges, and financial-literacy lessons.
why: Gamification can prompt action, while insight and education help users understand and sustain better financial decisions.
when: Building a finance experience intended to improve user capability as well as short-term engagement.
fails: Educational material is disconnected from the user’s current goals or analytics are too complex to act on.

claim: Offer badges for specific sustained behaviors, such as saving consistently for a defined number of days.
why: A clear threshold turns a habit into a recognisable achievement and gives users an intermediate milestone before a savings goal is complete.
when: Reinforcing repeat behavior within a goal-tracking product.
fails: Badges become excessive, vague, or reward activity that does not benefit the user.

claim: Use one shared reward currency across multiple product activities so progress in one area reinforces engagement in another.
why: Goals and completed educational quizzes both earn Fin Bits, and those points affect leaderboard standing.
when: A product has several desired behaviors that should contribute to a single sense of user progression.
fails: The behaviors have incompatible value or a shared score would encourage low-quality, exploitative, or superficial activity.

claim: Make progression legible with threshold-based states that clearly show promotion, neutral standing, and demotion risk.
why: The leaderboard divides users into visible ranges with distinct outcomes: promotion, no change, or relegation.
when: Users need to understand how current performance maps to a next status or tier.
fails: Ranking pressure would undermine the product's purpose or create harmful competition, especially around sensitive behaviors such as personal finance.

claim: Pair goal tracking with an immediately visible preview of the next reward to sustain momentum.
why: The goal screen displays current goals and lets users slide through the rewards available at later progress points.
when: A goal requires repeated effort over time and intermediate incentives can clarify what continued progress unlocks.
fails: Rewards distract from the primary goal or create expectations the product cannot consistently fulfill.

claim: Let users switch both the financial lens and time scale in analytics so the same screen supports different decisions.
why: The analytics view offers saving versus spending and daily, weekly, or monthly views.
when: A dataset needs to answer short-term behavior questions as well as longer-term planning questions.
fails: The available data is too sparse for granular periods or the controls create more options than users can interpret.

claim: Use a distinct alert color for exceptions against a target, and accompany it with actionable context.
why: Overspending periods are highlighted in purple, while recent transactions and upcoming-bill insights help the user understand and prepare for spending.
when: Users must identify deviations from a budget, target, or expected pattern quickly.
fails: Color is the only indicator, the meaning is ambiguous, or the alert state is applied so broadly that it becomes visual noise.

claim: Reward learning completion only after a lightweight knowledge check, then connect that reward back to the core progression system.
why: Lessons end with a quiz that earns Fin Bits, which in turn advances leaderboard status.
when: Educational content is intended to change user capability rather than merely accumulate views or clicks.
fails: The quiz is too easy to validate learning, too difficult for the lesson material, or rewards motivate answer-gaming over understanding.

claim: Create personas by consolidating research data into a realistic model of how a person experiences the specific product problem and solution.
why: A persona is useful only when it turns research into a decision-making reference for the design process.
when: Documenting research findings for a UX case study or using personas to guide product design.
fails: The persona is invented without supporting data or is not consulted during design decisions.

claim: Include persona details only when they affect the problem, solution, behavior, interests, goals, or pain points being designed for.
why: Irrelevant details add effort without improving design direction.
when: Choosing what fields and content belong in a persona.
fails: A seemingly peripheral attribute materially changes access needs, context of use, or decision-making.

claim: Make the user's goals and frustrations the most prominent parts of a persona.
why: These factors most directly reveal what the design needs to enable and reduce.
when: Structuring a persona for a defined product problem.

claim: Do not spend disproportionate effort choosing a persona name or photo; prioritize evidence-based behavioral content.
why: Cosmetic identity details do not meaningfully shape the design compared with research-derived needs and pain points.
when: Preparing personas under normal case-study constraints.
fails: Identity representation is required for a specific stakeholder, accessibility, or communication purpose.

claim: Use the persona's observed or research-supported behaviors, interests, and pain points to justify later design choices in the case study.
why: This creates a traceable connection from user research to design outcomes.
when: Explaining how research informed a proposed interface or product flow.
fails: The later design addresses a different audience or problem than the persona represents.
